body:
Meaning of nuclear command and control

Nuclear command and control refers to the institutional arrangements through which a country exercises authority over its nuclear forces, makes authorised decisions and maintains control over those forces.

These arrangements establish who is permitted to make decisions, which institutions provide information and advice, and how lawful political authority is maintained over strategic forces.

Nuclear command and control is especially important because the consequences of nuclear weapon use are extraordinarily severe. The decision to authorise nuclear use must therefore be distinguished from the routine military responsibility of maintaining and administering strategic capabilities.

Command and control: The system of authority, institutional responsibilities and controls governing decisions about nuclear forces and their authorised use.

India's Nuclear Command Authority

On 4 January 2003, India's Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) publicly set out important aspects of the country's nuclear doctrine and command arrangements.

The announcement identified the Nuclear Command Authority (NCA) as the mechanism through which civilian political leadership authorises nuclear retaliation.

The NCA comprises 2 councils: the Political Council and the Executive Council. Their functions are different.

Political Council

The Political Council is chaired by the Prime Minister of India.

According to the official announcement of 4 January 2003, the Political Council is the sole body authorised to approve the use of nuclear weapons.

This means that the authority to make the nuclear-use decision rests with civilian political leadership through the Political Council. It is not an independent decision belonging to an individual military service or a field commander.

Executive Council

The Executive Council is chaired by the National Security Advisor (NSA).

It provides inputs for decision-making by the Nuclear Command Authority and executes the directives issued by the Political Council.

The distinction between the councils is important. The Executive Council supports decision-making and carries out authorised directives, whereas the Political Council possesses the authority to approve nuclear use.

Strategic Forces Command

The 2003 announcement also approved the appointment of a Commander-in-Chief, Strategic Forces Command (SFC), to manage and administer India's strategic forces.

The Strategic Forces Command is therefore associated with the management and administration of strategic military capabilities. It must not be confused with the Political Council, which holds nuclear-use authorisation authority.

Why is civilian political control significant?

Civilian political control separates the final decision to authorise nuclear weapon use from the military responsibilities of maintaining and administering strategic forces.

It also places nuclear decisions within an identified national authority rather than leaving such decisions to individual personnel.

A credible deterrent requires not only military capability but also clear political authority. Potential adversaries must understand that the country's nuclear forces are governed by an established decision-making structure.

Command and control also supports safety and accountability by distinguishing authorised decisions from unauthorised action.

Doctrine, command and delivery: 3 different concepts

Three related questions help distinguish the main elements of nuclear policy:

  • Nuclear doctrine: What is the declared policy governing nuclear deterrence and the circumstances of nuclear use?
  • Nuclear command and control: Which institutions possess authority to make and implement decisions?
  • Nuclear delivery capability: What broad categories of systems provide the country's ability to deliver nuclear weapons?

For India, the no-first-use doctrine concerns declared policy; the Nuclear Command Authority concerns decision-making authority; and the nuclear triad concerns delivery capability.

The Nuclear Command Authority has 2 councils, not 3. The Strategic Forces Command is a distinct military command and should not be counted as a third council of the NCA.

Prelims focus

  • India's nuclear command arrangements were publicly described by the Cabinet Committee on Security on 4 January 2003.
  • The Nuclear Command Authority comprises the Political Council and Executive Council.
  • The Political Council is chaired by the Prime Minister.
  • The Political Council is the sole body authorised to approve nuclear weapon use.
  • The Executive Council is chaired by the National Security Advisor.
  • The Strategic Forces Command manages and administers strategic forces.
  • Trap: The National Security Advisor chairs the Executive Council, not the Political Council.

[Sources: Ministry of External Affairs, India's Foreign Relations 2003, General section, document 002, 'Press release of the Government of India on the review of the operationalization of India's Nuclear Doctrine by the Cabinet Committee on Security', 4 January 2003, printed p. 73, paragraphs 2–6; Press Information Bureau, Prime Minister's Office, 'Prime Minister felicitates crew of INS Arihant on completion of Nuclear Triad', 5 November 2018, release ID 1551894, paragraph on nuclear command and control, accessed 14 November 2026.]

title: Nuclear Command and Control: India's Civilian Decision-Making Structure

body:
What is a nuclear doctrine?

A nuclear doctrine is a country's stated set of principles concerning the role of nuclear weapons in national security, nuclear deterrence and the circumstances in which nuclear weapons may be used.

A doctrine explains the intended strategic role of nuclear weapons. It is different from the physical characteristics of weapons, the delivery platforms that carry them and the command institutions that exercise authority over them.

India's publicly declared nuclear policy is based on credible minimum deterrence and a no-first-use posture, with important qualifications set out in the official doctrine.

The official declaration of 4 January 2003

On 4 January 2003, the Government of India released an official statement following a review by the Cabinet Committee on Security.

This statement publicly summarised India's nuclear doctrine and the arrangements governing its nuclear forces.

The central principles may be understood as follows:

PrincipleMeaning
Credible minimum deterrenceMaintain a nuclear deterrent considered sufficient and believable for national security.
No First UseDeclare that nuclear weapons will not be used first in a nuclear confrontation, subject to the doctrine's stated qualification concerning major chemical or biological attacks.
Massive retaliationDeclare that nuclear retaliation to a first nuclear strike will be massive and designed to inflict unacceptable damage.
Civilian political authorisationRequire nuclear retaliatory attacks to be authorised by civilian political leadership through the Nuclear Command Authority.
Non-use against non-nuclear-weapon statesDeclare a general policy of not using nuclear weapons against states without nuclear weapons.

Credible minimum deterrence

Credible minimum deterrence combines 2 ideas.

Credible means that an adversary should believe the country retains a sufficient ability to retaliate and that the threat of retaliation is meaningful.

Minimum expresses the intention to maintain a deterrent adequate for the country's security requirements rather than treating the largest possible nuclear arsenal as the objective.

The word minimum does not establish a fixed number of nuclear weapons in India's public declaration. It refers to an approach based on maintaining an adequate and credible deterrent capability.

Credible minimum deterrence does not mean possessing the smallest possible number of weapons regardless of effectiveness. It means seeking a deterrent regarded as sufficient and credible for the intended security purpose.

India's No First Use doctrine

No First Use (NFU) means that a country declares it will not be the first to use nuclear weapons in a conflict.

India's official statement of 4 January 2003 specified that nuclear weapons would be used in retaliation against a nuclear attack on Indian territory or Indian forces anywhere.

This distinction matters because the declared retaliatory protection is not limited exclusively to attacks physically occurring inside India's territory.

Under the nuclear-retaliation principle, India declares that it will not initiate nuclear weapon use against an adversary. If the adversary launches a nuclear attack against Indian territory or Indian forces, the doctrine provides for nuclear retaliation.

However, the 2003 statement contains a separate and important qualification involving chemical and biological weapons, explained below.

Massive retaliation

The 2003 doctrine states that nuclear retaliation to a first nuclear strike will be massive and intended to cause unacceptable damage.

This is a declared deterrence posture. By communicating the prospect of very severe retaliation, it seeks to discourage an adversary from initiating nuclear use.

The term massive retaliation should not be confused with No First Use. They answer different questions:

  • No First Use: Which side initiates nuclear weapon use?
  • Massive retaliation: What character of nuclear response is declared after an adversary's first nuclear strike?

A country's declaration of no first use therefore does not mean it has renounced nuclear retaliation.

The chemical and biological weapons qualification

The 2003 statement also declared that, in the event of a major attack against India or Indian forces anywhere using biological or chemical weapons, India would retain the option of responding with nuclear weapons.

This is an important qualification to the general no-first-use posture.

It does not say that every chemical or biological incident must automatically lead to nuclear retaliation. The statement refers specifically to a major attack and preserves an option rather than establishing an automatic response.

Important qualification

India's 2003 doctrine declares No First Use in relation to nuclear attacks but expressly retains the option of nuclear retaliation following a major chemical or biological weapons attack against India or Indian forces anywhere. Therefore, describing the doctrine as an absolutely unconditional prohibition on all first nuclear use would be inaccurate.

Distinguishing No First Use from related policies

No First Use, non-use against non-nuclear-weapon states and nuclear disarmament are related but separate ideas.

  • No First Use: A declared restraint on initiating nuclear weapon use, subject to the stated qualification in India's doctrine.
  • Non-use against non-nuclear-weapon states: A declared general restraint concerning states that do not possess nuclear weapons, also stated in the 2003 doctrine.
  • Nuclear disarmament: The reduction and eventual elimination of nuclear weapons.

India has also declared support for global, verifiable and non-discriminatory nuclear disarmament. Supporting nuclear disarmament is not the same as declaring that a country currently possesses no nuclear weapons.

Important developments in India's declared policy

Several dated developments help distinguish India's nuclear capability, draft policy, official doctrine and subsequent reaffirmations.

  • May 1998: India conducted a series of nuclear tests demonstrating its nuclear weapons capability.
  • August 1999: A draft nuclear doctrine was released for public discussion. A draft should not be confused with the subsequent official declaration.
  • 4 January 2003: The Cabinet Committee on Security publicly set out the official nuclear doctrine and nuclear command arrangements.
  • 5 November 2018: The Government of India announced INS Arihant's first deterrence patrol and described the development as completing India's survivable nuclear triad.
  • 20 May 2026: In an official Ministry of Defence press release, India's Defence Minister expressly reaffirmed the country's commitment to No First Use.

India's stated policy at the content cutoff

For a content cutoff of 14 November 2026, the relevant dated official position includes the Ministry of Defence statement issued through the Press Information Bureau on 20 May 2026.

In that statement, India's Defence Minister reaffirmed that India adheres to the No First Use policy and remains committed to it.

An earlier official statement by India's representative to the First Committee of the United Nations General Assembly, delivered on 15 October 2025, likewise reaffirmed credible minimum deterrence, No First Use and non-use against non-nuclear-weapon states.

The 2003 Cabinet Committee on Security declaration remains the essential dated reference for understanding the detailed principles and qualifications described in this lesson. The 2025 and 2026 official statements provide subsequent public reaffirmation of the central declared posture.

Connecting the doctrine with deterrence and the nuclear triad

The complete relationship can now be understood.

India's credible minimum deterrence policy concerns the intended sufficiency and credibility of its nuclear deterrent. Its No First Use posture concerns the declared conditions for nuclear use. Its nuclear triad provides different categories of delivery capability that can help sustain the deterrent.

The Nuclear Command Authority supplies the civilian political decision-making structure, while the Strategic Forces Command has responsibility for managing and administering strategic forces.

These are distinct but connected elements of national nuclear policy. A correct understanding requires distinguishing the purpose of deterrence, the physical capability, the delivery platforms, the conditions of use and the authority responsible for decisions.

Prelims focus

  • India's official nuclear doctrine was publicly set out by the Cabinet Committee on Security on 4 January 2003.
  • Its central principles include credible minimum deterrence and No First Use.
  • The doctrine declares massive nuclear retaliation to a first nuclear strike.
  • Its stated nuclear-retaliation protection covers Indian territory and Indian forces anywhere.
  • India's 2003 doctrine retains the option of nuclear retaliation in the event of a major chemical or biological weapons attack.
  • The Ministry of Defence officially reaffirmed India's No First Use policy on 20 May 2026.
  • Trap: No First Use does not mean never using nuclear weapons. Nor does the chemical and biological weapons qualification make nuclear retaliation automatic.

[Sources: Ministry of External Affairs, India's Foreign Relations 2003, General section, document 002, 'Press release of the Government of India on the review of the operationalization of India's Nuclear Doctrine by the Cabinet Committee on Security', 4 January 2003, printed pp. 72–73; NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class 12, Chapter 4, 'India's External Relations', printed pp. 78–79; Manpreet Sethi, 'India's No First Use Nuclear Doctrine', Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses, discussion of the 1999 draft and 2003 declaration, 2019, accessed 14 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Prime Minister's Office, 'Prime Minister felicitates crew of INS Arihant on completion of Nuclear Triad', 5 November 2018, release ID 1551894, accessed 14 November 2026; Ministry of External Affairs, statement by India's Permanent Representative to the Conference on Disarmament at the First Committee of the 80th United Nations General Assembly, delivered 15 October 2025, paragraphs on nuclear disarmament and India's nuclear doctrine, accessed 14 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Raksha Mantri holds bilateral talks with Minister of National Defence, Republic of Korea in Seoul', 20 May 2026, release ID 2263304, paragraph on India's No First Use policy, accessed 14 November 2026.]
